checkpoints: Elasticsearch is near-real-time rather than real-time: a document written via an index call becomes durable immediately, but it only becomes searchable after the next refresh cycle, which by default fires roughly once per second.

Because the index call in question uses the default refresh: false, a search issued immediately afterward races against that periodic refresh cycle instead of against a guaranteed-consistent index state.

The intermittent pass/fail pattern is a timing race, not a deterministic defect in the write path — whether the search lands before or after the refresh has already fired depends on incidental wall-clock delays like network round-trip and test-runner scheduling.

"The write is lost" and "the write is not yet visible to search" are different claims; the document is never dropped or corrupted, so treating this as data loss sends debugging effort toward the wrong root cause.

Setting refresh: "wait_for" on the index call is the correct fix for this read-after-write case: it blocks the write's response until the document becomes searchable by riding the next refresh cycle, without forcing an extra one.
Using refresh: true forces an immediate refresh on every write, which increases I/O cost and interferes with segment merging under load, so it is not a good default for fixing this.

refresh: "wait_for" (or an explicit index refresh) belongs on read-after-write paths like tests or specific user-facing flows, not on every production write, since it still adds latency compared to the default asynchronous refresh: false.
Confirming the fix requires re-running the seed-then-search flow repeatedly rather than trusting a single passing run, since one pass does not prove the race condition is actually closed.
